Lateral swelling/bruising.text: Localized swelling and ecchymosis over the lateral malleolus reflect capsular/ligamentous hemorrhage from the ATFL (and CFL if more severe) following an inversion mechanism; the lateral (not diffuse or medial) distribution supports a classic inversion-sprain pattern.

antalgic gait.text: A pain-guarded limp reflects protective offloading of the injured lateral ligament complex; inability to bear weight for four steps immediately after injury and at examination is also one of the Ottawa Ankle Rules criteria used to screen for fracture.
antalgic gait.source: Stiell et al., Ottawa Ankle Rules validation studies

Guarded plantarflexed posture.text: Resting the foot in slight plantarflexion shortens/unloads the ATFL, which is under greatest tension in plantarflexion combined with inversion — a protective position that minimizes strain on the acutely injured ligament.

passive.label: Passive Inversion (subtalar joint)
options: Pain reproduced with laxity (ATFL/CFL torn — talar tilt)

findings: Resisted eversion (peroneals) often weak/painful acutely — protective reflex inhibition, not necessarily a tear
Passive inversion (STJ) reproduces pain, with laxity present if ATFL/CFL torn (talar tilt)
sttt.interpretation: Resisted eversion weakness acutely reflects protective reflex inhibition, not necessarily a structural tear; passive inversion reproducing pain with laxity confirms ATFL/CFL involvement via the talar-tilt mechanism.

cpa.pattern: Peroneals are typically inhibited/reflex-guarded acutely; as healing progresses, check for an overactive-peroneals / inhibited-tib-ant pattern feeding recurrent instability. Fascial component (from source): Lateral ligament / peroneal fascia.

kineticChain.name: Subtalar Joint Mobility (Inversion/Eversion)
kineticChain.chainEffect: The direct match to ATFL/CFL sprain mechanics; expect acute guarding rather than a fixed hypo/hypermobility pattern yet.

functionalScreen.name: Single Leg Balance (proprioception + CAI screen)
functionalScreen.note: Once acute swelling allows — too early acutely, but the baseline test to schedule for follow-up. FMA source note: Anterior-drawer/talar-tilt & single-leg balance deficit.

Recurrent swelling.text: Repeated bouts of effusion following minor perturbation reflect ongoing mechanical and functional insufficiency of the lateral ligament complex rather than a single acute event — a hallmark distinguishing CAI from an isolated acute sprain.
Recurrent swelling.source: International Ankle Consortium consensus statement on chronic ankle instability

feeling of giving way.text: Subjective instability ("giving way") is a core diagnostic criterion for CAI per International Ankle Consortium consensus, reflecting a combination of residual mechanical laxity and impaired neuromuscular/proprioceptive control rather than structural failure alone.

Rearfoot varus / supinated posture.text: A varus-aligned, supinated rearfoot sits closer to the inverted position that loads the lateral ligaments, both predisposing to recurrent sprain and reflecting the altered loading pattern that perpetuates instability.

findings: Resisted eversion often weak — peroneal weakness/reflex inhibition well documented in CAI
Passive inversion shows excess/hypermobile range — the opposite of a capsular restriction
sttt.interpretation: Peroneal weakness/reflex inhibition on resisted eversion is well documented in CAI; passive inversion showing excessive/hypermobile range (the opposite of a capsular restriction) confirms mechanical laxity rather than stiffness.

muscles.name: Peroneals
muscles.state: Overactive, tib ant inhibition — OR — simple weakness/delay (cross-check both)

cpa.pattern: Check both an "Overactive, tib ant inhibition" pattern AND simple peroneal weakness/delay — this cross-check is the key CPA question in chronic instability. Fascial component (from source): Peroneal fascial support; subtalar mobility.

kineticChain.name: Subtalar Joint Mobility
kineticChain.chainEffect: Expect "hypermobile, excessive pronation" or a marked L-vs-R asymmetry, per this app's own documented CAI presentation.

functionalScreen.name: Single Leg Balance (proprioception + CAI screen)
functionalScreen.note: The named functional test for exactly this condition. FMA source note: Star-excursion balance deficit, single-leg stance failure.

Swelling above joint line.text: Swelling extending proximal to the ankle mortise, over the distal tibiofibular syndesmosis and interosseous membrane, rather than confined to the lateral malleolus, is a key sign distinguishing a syndesmotic injury from a lateral (ATFL/CFL) sprain.
Swelling above joint line.source: Williams & Allen, Ankle Syndesmosis Injuries: Anatomy, Biomechanics, Mechanism of Injury, JOSPT 2006

pain on squeeze.text: A positive squeeze test — pain reproduced at the syndesmosis when the tibia and fibula are compressed together proximally — occurs because the compressive force is transmitted distally, separating the fibula from the tibia at an already-injured, less stable mortise.
pain on squeeze.source: Teitz & Harrington, Biomechanical Analysis of the Squeeze Test, Am J Sports Med 1998

Externally-rotated foot guarding.text: Holding the foot externally rotated avoids the combined external-rotation/dorsiflexion motion that widens the mortise and stresses the injured syndesmotic ligaments — the same mechanism the external rotation stress test deliberately reproduces.

passive.label: External Rotation Stress + Squeeze (proximal tib-fib compression)

findings: Passive external-rotation stress + squeeze (proximal tib-fib compression) reproduces high (syndesmotic) pain — the definitive joint-play test here, not a resisted-muscle one
sttt.interpretation: Resisted dorsiflexion/plantarflexion are less specific in a high ankle sprain; the passive external-rotation stress and squeeze (proximal tib-fib compression) tests are the definitive joint-play findings.

cpa.reason: Not primarily compensation-driven (ligamentous/syndesmotic) — reassess Tib Ant/Peroneal balance once healed; prolonged non-weight-bearing can inhibit both. Fascial component (from source): Interosseous membrane / distal syndesmotic fascia.

kineticChain.reason: Not covered by this app's talocrural/subtalar kinetic-chain tests (a syndesmosis is a separate joint) — rely on the squeeze/external-rotation stress tests above.

functionalScreen.name: Weight-Bearing Dorsiflexion (Knee-to-Wall)
functionalScreen.note: Syndesmotic widening affects mortise dorsiflexion mechanics even though it isn't the primary named screen for this injury. FMA source note: Squeeze & external-rotation stress reproduce high pain.

Tendon thickening/tenderness.text: Fusiform thickening reflects chronic tendinosis — collagen disorganization and neovascularization — rather than an acute inflammatory tendinitis; tenderness localizing to either the mid-portion or the insertion guides the differentiation made on palpation.
Tendon thickening/tenderness.source: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Ch.13; VISA-A development, Robinson et al. 2001

calf wasting.text: Wasting reflects chronic disuse and reflexive inhibition of gastrocnemius-soleus from pain avoidance, which further reduces the muscle-tendon unit's shock-absorbing capacity and can perpetuate tendon overload.

Overpronation increasing tendon load.text: Excessive subtalar pronation produces a whipping/bowstring effect on the Achilles as it inserts medially on the calcaneus, increasing shear and torsional load through the tendon — a well-documented contributor to tendinopathy.

Achilles tendon — insertional.text: Tenderness at the calcaneal insertion implicates insertional Achilles tendinopathy, often with a concurrent retrocalcaneal bursitis or Haglund's deformity, a distinct entity from mid-portion disease requiring different loading strategies.
Achilles tendon — insertional.source: VISA-A literature, Robinson et al. 2001; Magee, Ch.13

Achilles tendon — mid-portion.text: Tenderness 2–6cm proximal to the insertion localizes to the tendon's relatively hypovascular "watershed" zone, the most common site of mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy.

passive.label: Passive Dorsiflexion — knee extended vs flexed

findings: Resisted plantarflexion strong but painful at the tendon — classic contractile pattern
Passive dorsiflexion better with knee flexed = gastroc (vs soleus) differentiation
sttt.interpretation: Strong-but-painful resisted plantarflexion at the tendon is the classic contractile pattern; comparing passive dorsiflexion with the knee extended vs flexed differentiates a gastrocnemius vs soleus tightness contribution.

cpa.pattern: Gastrocnemius/Soleus overactivity compensates for an inhibited Glute Max at the hip; reduced glute-driven propulsion increases calf load. Fascial component (from source): Superficial back line (gastroc-soleus-Achilles).

kineticChain.name: Weight-Bearing Dorsiflexion Lunge Test
kineticChain.chainEffect: Restricted dorsiflexion directly increases Achilles load; gastroc/soleus tightness is explicitly named as a driver of this restriction.

functionalScreen.name: Single Leg Heel Raise (calf endurance)
functionalScreen.note: The direct named functional test for this exact condition. FMA source note: Single-leg heel-raise load & hop reproduce tendon pain.

AF05.name: Achilles Tendon Rupture (Complete)

Palpable gap.text: A palpable defect in the tendon substance, typically 2–6cm proximal to the insertion, is direct evidence of complete structural discontinuity, although rapidly developing swelling can mask the gap within hours of injury.

positive Thompson.text: Absence of plantarflexion when the calf is passively squeezed confirms loss of mechanical continuity between gastrocnemius-soleus and the calcaneus. Because it does not rely on active contraction, Thompson's (Simmond's) test remains valid even when pain inhibits voluntary effort, and it is the definitive confirmatory sign of complete rupture.
positive Thompson.source: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Ch.13 (Thompson/Simmond's test)

bruising.text: Ecchymosis tracking down the posterior calf and ankle reflects hemorrhage from the torn tendon and surrounding paratenon, consistent with a recent complete rupture.

Cannot toe-off.text: Loss of the mechanical link between the calf and calcaneus means the ankle can no longer generate the plantarflexion force required for push-off — a functional hallmark of complete Achilles rupture. This is an acute presentation requiring urgent orthopaedic referral, not further mechanical stress testing.

flat gait.text: A compensatory flat-footed, shuffling gait avoids the terminal-stance plantarflexion phase that the ruptured tendon can no longer power, substituting hip and knee strategies for the lost ankle push-off.

Palpable tendon gap.text: A discrete palpable defect in the tendon, usually 2–6cm proximal to the calcaneal insertion, is one of the most specific direct signs of a complete rupture and should prompt urgent orthopaedic referral rather than further mechanical testing.

findings: Resisted plantarflexion absent/severely weak with a palpable gap
Thompson's/Simmond's (passive calf squeeze) is the definitive test — not active resisted testing
sttt.interpretation: A palpable gap with absent/severely weak resisted plantarflexion, confirmed by a positive Thompson's/Simmond's test (passive calf squeeze — the definitive test here, not active resisted testing), indicates a complete Achilles rupture. Urgent orthopaedic referral, not manipulation or end-range testing.

cpa.reason: Not applicable acutely — urgent orthopaedic referral takes priority over compensation-pattern testing. Fascial component (from source): N/A — urgent referral.

functionalScreen.reason: Not applicable acutely — a Single Leg Heel Raise attempt would be diagnostic by its complete failure, but formal functional testing is deferred to urgent referral. FMA source note: Single-leg heel-raise impossible; Thompson positive.

outcomeMeasures: N/A — acute/medical; functional outcome once appropriate

AF06.name: Ankle Osteoarthritis
keyExams: Imaging referral if not already available

Anterior joint-line swelling.text: Synovial effusion and soft-tissue swelling anterior to the talocrural joint reflects reactive synovitis secondary to degenerative articular change, most visible where the joint capsule lies most superficial.

reduced DF.text: Anterior tibiotalar osteophyte formation mechanically blocks the talar dome from gliding posteriorly during dorsiflexion, producing a hard bony restriction of dorsiflexion that can coexist with — and is distinct from — the classic capsular pattern in which plantarflexion is more globally limited than dorsiflexion.
reduced DF.source: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Ch.13 (capsular pattern of the talocrural joint)

crepitus.text: Palpable or audible crepitus during range of motion reflects irregular, degenerated articular cartilage surfaces grinding against each other — a hallmark sign of osteoarthritic joint change.

Stiff antalgic posture.text: A globally guarded, stiff gait and resting posture reflects pain avoidance of end-range joint positions that compress the degenerated articular surfaces, minimizing symptomatic loading during weight-bearing.

findings: Resisted tests generally painless — non-contractile pattern
Passive DF/PF restricted in a capsular pattern (PF>DF) with a hard/bony end-feel
sttt.interpretation: Painless resisted testing rules out a contractile source; a capsular-pattern restriction (plantarflexion more limited than dorsiflexion) with a hard/bony end-feel is consistent with osteoarthritic change.

cpa.pattern: Gastrocnemius/Soleus are often overactive/shortened, restricting dorsiflexion — check alongside Tibialis Anterior for an anterior-impingement contribution. Fascial component (from source): Anterior capsular fascia.

kineticChain.name: Weight-Bearing Dorsiflexion Lunge Test
kineticChain.chainEffect: Expect severe restriction (<4cm / <10°), consistent with OA-related capsular loss.

functionalScreen.name: Weight-Bearing Dorsiflexion (Knee-to-Wall)
functionalScreen.note: The same test named as the functional screen for ankle DF restriction, impingement, and OA. FMA source note: Weight-bearing lunge restricted; stairs limited.

Medial swelling.text: Swelling tracking along the medial ankle and hindfoot follows the course of the tibialis posterior tendon behind the medial malleolus, reflecting tenosynovitis or tendinosis at the primary site of pathology.

“too-many-toes”.text: Viewed from behind, forefoot abduction relative to the hindfoot — secondary to collapse of the medial longitudinal arch and hindfoot valgus as tibialis posterior fails to control pronation — exposes more of the lateral toes than normal. This is the classic positive "too-many-toes" sign of posterior tibial tendon insufficiency.
“too-many-toes”.source: StatPearls, Posterior Tibial Tendon Dysfunction; Physio-pedia, PTTD

collapsing arch.text: Progressive loss of the medial longitudinal arch reflects failure of tibialis posterior's primary dynamic function of supporting the arch during the stance phase of gait, allowing the midfoot to collapse into pronation unchecked.

Hindfoot valgus / flatfoot posture.text: A valgus-collapsed hindfoot is the static consequence of chronic tibialis posterior insufficiency, since the tendon normally inverts and stabilizes the subtalar joint against the pronating ground-reaction force during stance.
Hindfoot valgus / flatfoot posture.source: AAOS, Progressive Collapsing Foot Deformity; StatPearls PTTD

findings: Resisted inversion (tib post) weak
Single-leg heel raise fails to invert the heel — the functional resisted-test equivalent
Navicular drop quantifies the arch collapse
sttt.interpretation: Weak resisted inversion (tibialis posterior) combined with a single-leg heel raise that fails to invert the heel is the functional resisted-test equivalent; navicular drop then quantifies the degree of arch collapse.

cpa.pattern: Tibialis Posterior inhibition (progressive flatfoot) with overactive Peroneals is the textbook PTTD compensation pattern, explicitly documented. Fascial component (from source): Deep posterior-compartment fascia (tib-post).

kineticChain.name: Subtalar Joint Mobility

fields.label: Subtalar mobility pattern
options: Hypermobile, excessive pronation — tibialis posterior failing to control pronation

kineticChain.chainEffect: "Hypermobile, excessive pronation... tibialis posterior failing to control pronation" is the exact documented pattern for this condition.

functionalScreen.name: Dynamic Arch / Navicular Drop
functionalScreen.note: Tibialis posterior function + foot pronation screen — the named functional test for exactly this condition. FMA source note: Single-leg heel-raise fails to invert heel; resisted inversion weak.

AF08.name: Peroneal Tendinopathy
keyExams: Peroneal tendon palpation behind lateral malleolus

Retromalleolar swelling/tenderness.text: Swelling and tenderness behind the lateral malleolus track the peroneus longus and brevis tendons through the fibular groove, the site most vulnerable to friction-related tendinopathy and subluxation.

Rearfoot varus (overload) posture.text: A varus-aligned rearfoot increases the mechanical demand placed on the peroneals — the primary evertors and lateral dynamic stabilizers that must counteract the varus alignment — predisposing the tendons to overload tendinopathy.

Peroneal tendon — behind lateral malleol.text: Point tenderness directly over the peroneal tendons posterior to the lateral malleolus, their anatomic course through the retromalleolar groove, localizes the lesion to the tendons rather than the lateral ligament complex — an important differentiation from an acute lateral ankle sprain.

findings: Resisted eversion strong but painful behind the lateral malleolus — classic contractile pattern
Subluxation provocation (resisted eversion + DF) is the joint-play analogue
sttt.interpretation: Strong-but-painful resisted eversion behind the lateral malleolus is the classic contractile pattern for peroneal tendinopathy; the subluxation provocation test (resisted eversion + dorsiflexion) is the joint-play analogue used to screen for tendon instability.

muscles.name: Peroneals
muscles.state: Overactive, tib ant inhibition — OR — tib post inhibition (determine which)

cpa.pattern: Determine WHICH muscle the peroneals are compensating for — tibialis anterior inhibition or tibialis posterior inhibition — before treating the peroneals in isolation. Fascial component (from source): Lateral (peroneal) compartment fascia.

kineticChain.name: Subtalar Joint Mobility (adjunct context)
kineticChain.chainEffect: Not the primary test for this condition, but useful adjunct context since peroneals stabilise subtalar eversion — informs the compensation pattern noted in CPA above.

functionalScreen.name: Single Leg Heel Raise (observe heel-eversion quality)
functionalScreen.note: The app has no peroneal-specific named functional screen, so this tib-post-oriented test is used as the closest adjunct. FMA source note: Resisted eversion & single-leg balance reproduce lateral pain.

Medial-ankle Tinel.text: A positive Tinel's sign — tingling or paresthesia reproduced by percussion over the tibial nerve posterior to the medial malleolus — indicates an irritable or compressed nerve at the tarsal tunnel, the classic provocative sign of this entrapment neuropathy.
Medial-ankle Tinel.source: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Ch.13 (Tinel's sign)

intrinsic wasting.text: Wasting of the intrinsic foot musculature, innervated by the medial and lateral plantar nerves (branches of the tibial nerve distal to the tunnel), reflects chronic motor denervation from sustained tibial nerve compression.

Overpronation compressing the tunnel.text: Sustained pronation stretches and narrows the tarsal tunnel, which is bordered by the flexor retinaculum, increasing pressure on the tibial nerve and its branches — the documented mechanical driver of this entrapment.

findings: Resisted inversion/PF generally preserved — neural, not contractile pattern
Tinel's sign + sustained eversion-dorsiflexion is the key provocation; sensory mapping of the plantar foot confirms the distribution
sttt.interpretation: Preserved resisted strength points to a neural rather than contractile source; Tinel's sign combined with sustained eversion-dorsiflexion provocation is the key finding, with sensory mapping of the plantar foot confirming the nerve distribution involved.

cpa.reason: Not a classic muscle-pair pattern (nerve entrapment) — check for overpronation (Tib Post inhibition) as the mechanical driver compressing the tunnel. Fascial component (from source): Flexor retinaculum / tibial neural tension.

kineticChain.reason: Not a joint-mobility condition (nerve entrapment); Subtalar Mobility can be checked as the mechanical driver of the overpronation noted in CPA above.

functionalScreen.name: Dynamic Arch / Navicular Drop
functionalScreen.note: Overpronation is the documented mechanical driver compressing the tunnel, matching the CPA finding above. FMA source note: Sustained eversion-dorsiflexion & Tinel reproduce burning.

AF10.name: Anterior Ankle Impingement
keyExams: Weight-bearing dorsiflexion lunge test w/ anterior pain provocation

Anterior joint-line tenderness.text: Tenderness directly over the anterior talocrural joint line localizes to anterior tibiotalar osteophytes or hypertrophic synovial/capsular tissue that becomes pinched between the tibia and talar neck during dorsiflexion.

dorsiflexion block.text: A firm mechanical block to dorsiflexion, rather than a gradual stretch-type restriction, reflects direct bony or soft-tissue impingement as the talus attempts to glide posteriorly beneath the tibia during dorsiflexion.

Restricted-DF stiff posture.text: A gait or resting posture that avoids terminal dorsiflexion reflects functional avoidance of the anterior pinch mechanism that reproduces pain during weight-bearing dorsiflexion.

findings: Resisted dorsiflexion may reproduce anterior pinch pain if soft-tissue impingement is present
Passive dorsiflexion end-feel is HARD/bony (bony impingement) — differentiates from a simple gastroc-tightness DF restriction
sttt.interpretation: A hard/bony passive dorsiflexion end-feel is the key distinction separating bony anterior impingement from a simple gastrocnemius-tightness dorsiflexion restriction; resisted dorsiflexion reproducing anterior pinch pain instead points to a soft-tissue impingement component.

cpa.pattern: Gastrocnemius/Soleus overactivity restricting available dorsiflexion increases anterior joint approximation — check calf length/activation alongside the joint pathology itself. Fascial component (from source): Anterior capsular / talar fascial pinch.

kineticChain.name: Weight-Bearing Dorsiflexion Lunge Test
kineticChain.chainEffect: The direct match for this condition — expect restricted dorsiflexion with anterior pinch pain reproduced during the lunge.

functionalScreen.name: Weight-Bearing Dorsiflexion (Knee-to-Wall)
functionalScreen.note: The same test, whose own subtitle names "impingement + CAI screen" as its purpose. FMA source note: Weight-bearing lunge blocked/painful anteriorly.

AF11.name: Plantar Fasciitis / Plantar Fasciopathy
keyExams: Palpation — medial calcaneal tubercle / fascia origin

Medial calcaneal tenderness.text: Tenderness at the medial calcaneal tubercle localizes to the origin of the plantar fascia, the site of maximal tensile and traction stress — and consequent micro-tearing — in plantar fasciopathy.

antalgic heel-strike.text: Avoidance of forceful heel-strike reflects pain-guarded loading of the inflamed/degenerated fascia origin, and is classically worst with the first steps after rest, when the fascia has shortened overnight and is then abruptly stretched under load.

High or collapsed arch.text: A high-arched (pes cavus) foot has poor shock absorption and leaves the fascia under greater resting tension, while a collapsed, pronated arch increases fascia strain through sustained elongation — both extremes of arch posture raise tensile load on the plantar fascia via different biomechanical pathways.

overpronation.text: Excessive pronation elongates the medial longitudinal arch during stance, increasing tensile strain on the plantar fascia with every step — one of the principal mechanical drivers of plantar fasciopathy.

Medial calcaneal tubercle / fascia origi.text: Direct palpation reproducing pain precisely at the fascia's calcaneal origin is the classic and most sensitive palpation finding for plantar fasciitis, helping differentiate it from a central heel-pad or nerve-based cause of heel pain.

findings: Not a classic resisted-muscle test — fascia, not contractile — resisted toe flexion (FHL) is usually painless
Windlass test (passive great-toe dorsiflexion, weight-bearing) is the definitive provocation
sttt.interpretation: Plantar fasciitis is not a classic resisted-muscle (contractile) pattern — resisted toe flexion (FHL) is usually painless. The Windlass test (passive great-toe dorsiflexion, weight-bearing) is the definitive provocation.

cpa.pattern: FHL inhibition is the exact documented driver — the fascia takes over arch-support duty the FHL should share. Fascial component (from source): Superficial back line (plantar-fascia ↔ gastroc).

kineticChain.name: First MTP Extension — Hallux Mobility
kineticChain.chainEffect: This app's own windlass test — dorsiflex the great toe on a step and observe the arch rise — is the direct kinetic-chain correlate for plantar fasciitis.

functionalScreen.name: Dynamic Arch / Navicular Drop
functionalScreen.note: The closest named screen — this app has no foot-specific FMA region, only Ankle — but arch mechanics overlap enough to be informative here. FMA source note: Windlass on single-toe stand reproduces heel pain. Also referenced in KEY EXAMS: Gait / arch assessment.

AF12.name: Heel Fat Pad Syndrome
keyExams: Palpation of central weight-bearing heel pad (vs medial origin)
palpation: Central weight-bearing heel pad (vs medial origin)

Central heel tenderness.text: Tenderness centered under the weight-bearing portion of the calcaneus, rather than at the medial fascia origin, localizes the lesion to the heel fat pad itself — the primary shock absorber during heel strike.

thin heel pad.text: A palpably thinned or atrophied fat pad — age-related, from chronic overload, or from prior corticosteroid injection — reduces the heel's natural shock-absorbing capacity, directly increasing impact stress transmitted to the calcaneus with every step.

Neutral arch; barefoot hard-surface load.text: A neutral, non-pathological arch combined with a history of barefoot or hard-surface loading indicates the pain is mechanically load-related rather than driven by an arch deformity — supporting fat-pad overload rather than a fasciopathy or structural foot deformity as the source.

Central weight-bearing heel pad (vs medi.text: Tenderness localizing to the central weight-bearing pad rather than the medial calcaneal tubercle is the key palpatory differentiator from plantar fasciitis, confirming the fat pad itself — not the fascia origin — as the pain generator.

passive.label: Direct Palpation — Central Heel Pad vs Medial Fascia Origin

findings: Not a resisted-muscle test — direct palpation of the central weight-bearing heel pad (vs the plantar fascia's medial origin) differentiates the two conditions
No windlass reproduction — differentiates from plantar fasciitis
sttt.interpretation: Direct palpation differentiates the central weight-bearing heel pad (fat-pad syndrome) from the plantar fascia's medial origin (plantar fasciitis); the absence of windlass-test reproduction further differentiates heel fat pad syndrome from plantar fasciitis.

cpa.reason: Not a compensation-pattern condition (fat-pad atrophy/loading) — footwear cushioning is the primary intervention, not muscle activation. Fascial component (from source): Plantar fat-pad / heel fascia.

kineticChain.reason: Not a joint-mobility condition (fat-pad atrophy) — none of this app's foot/ankle kinetic-chain tests target the heel pad specifically.

functionalScreen.reason: Not a functional-movement condition — direct palpation comparison (STTT, above) is the primary tool, not a named FMA screen. Barefoot vs cushioned-footwear comparison (from KEY EXAMS) is the practical adjunct. FMA source note: Deep central heel pressure (not medial origin) reproduces pain.

3rd/4th web-space tenderness.text: Tenderness localized to the third interspace, the most common site, reflects compression and entrapment of the common plantar digital nerve, which is thicker here from the confluence of branches of the medial and lateral plantar nerves and becomes trapped against the transverse intermetatarsal ligament as it passes between the metatarsal heads.
3rd/4th web-space tenderness.source: StatPearls, Morton Neuroma; Orthobullets, Interdigital (Morton's) Neuroma

splayed toes.text: Patients often splay or hold the toes apart to widen the forefoot and reduce compressive/traction load on the entrapped interdigital nerve — a common adaptive, protective posture.

Narrow-toe-box / forefoot-loading postur.text: Footwear or gait patterns that increase forefoot loading (narrow toe box, high heels) compress the metatarsal heads together and against the transverse intermetatarsal ligament, mechanically loading the confined space the interdigital nerve passes through — the primary documented driver of Morton's neuroma, per both the entrapment and chronic-microtrauma theories.

passive.label: Mulder's Click (passive mediolateral squeeze + interspace pressure)

findings: Not a resisted-muscle test — neural/interdigital — Mulder's click (passive mediolateral squeeze) is the definitive provocation
Web-space sensory testing maps the distribution
sttt.interpretation: Morton's neuroma is not tested with resisted-muscle testing since it is a neural/interdigital condition; Mulder's click (passive mediolateral squeeze with interspace pressure) is the definitive provocation, with web-space sensory testing mapping the distribution.

cpa.reason: Not a classic compensation pattern — narrow toe-box loading is mechanically driven; Foot Intrinsics facilitation is a supportive adjunct only. Fascial component (from source): Intermetatarsal fascia / plantar digital nerve.

kineticChain.reason: Not a joint-mobility condition (interdigital nerve) — none of the foot/ankle kinetic-chain tests isolate the web spaces.

functionalScreen.reason: Not applicable — Mulder's click (STTT, above) is the primary provocation, not a functional-movement screen. Toe-box footwear review (from KEY EXAMS) is the practical adjunct. FMA source note: Mulder's squeeze click; web-space sensory change.

AF14.name: Metatarsalgia (Mechanical Forefoot Overload)
keyExams: Palpation of metatarsal heads / plantar plate

Plantar callus under metatarsal heads.text: Hyperkeratotic callus formation directly under one or more metatarsal heads reflects chronically excessive, focal plantar pressure at that site — a marker of mechanical forefoot overload, often from an abnormal weight-distribution pattern such as an elevated or plantarflexed metatarsal or intrinsic muscle weakness.

Forefoot-loading / high-heel posture.text: Postures and footwear that shift body weight anteriorly onto the metatarsal heads — heeled shoes, a forefoot-strike gait — directly increase the compressive load under the forefoot, the mechanical driver of metatarsalgia.

Metatarsal heads / plantar plate.text: Direct tenderness over one or more metatarsal heads and the plantar plate localizes the site of mechanical overload; a positive dorsal drawer at this site would further suggest plantar plate insufficiency contributing to the overload pattern.

passive.label: Forefoot Loading (single-leg heel raise) — reproduces pain under metatarsal heads

findings: Resisted toe flexion/extension usually painless
Forefoot loading (single-leg heel raise) reproducing pain under the metatarsal heads is the functional provocation
sttt.interpretation: Resisted toe flexion/extension is usually painless in metatarsalgia; forefoot loading via a single-leg heel raise that reproduces pain under the metatarsal heads is the functional provocation test.

cpa.pattern: Foot intrinsic inhibition (arch collapse) often allows excess forefoot loading — check short-foot exercise capacity. Fascial component (from source): Plantar plate / forefoot fascia.

kineticChain.name: First MTP Extension — Hallux Mobility (adjunct context)
kineticChain.chainEffect: Restricted hallux extension shifts load laterally onto the metatarsal heads, feeding this exact metatarsalgia pattern.

functionalScreen.name: Single Leg Heel Raise (closest adjunct — observe foot-loading tolerance)
functionalScreen.note: This app has no dedicated forefoot-loading functional test — the ankle-region Single Leg Heel Raise is used as the closest adjunct to observe foot-loading tolerance. FMA source note: Single-leg heel-raise & forefoot load reproduce pain.

Dorsal 1st-MTP osteophyte.text: A palpable or visible dorsal osteophyte at the first metatarsal head reflects bony remodeling in response to chronic dorsal jamming of the joint during gait, and itself becomes an additional mechanical block to further dorsiflexion.

reduced toe extension.text: Progressive loss of first MTP dorsiflexion — normal gait requires roughly 65° at toe-off — reflects the combination of dorsal osteophyte impingement and plantar capsular contracture that defines hallux rigidus, directly impairing the terminal-stance push-off phase of gait.
reduced toe extension.source: StatPearls, Hallux Rigidus; Lower Extremity Review, Functional Hallux Limitus

Supinated / lateral-loading gait avoidin.text: Patients shift weight to the lateral border of the foot and avoid rolling through the restricted, painful first MTP joint at toe-off — a compensatory gait adaptation directly driven by the loss of first-MTP dorsiflexion.

passive.label: Passive 1st MTP Dorsiflexion
options: Most restricted — capsular pattern extension > flexion

findings: Resisted great-toe extension (EHL) may be painful at end-range
Passive 1st MTP dorsiflexion is MOST restricted in a capsular pattern (extension > flexion) with a hard/bony end-feel
Grind test confirms
sttt.interpretation: Passive 1st MTP dorsiflexion is the most restricted direction in a capsular pattern (extension more limited than flexion) with a hard/bony end-feel; the grind/axial compression test confirms a joint (not tendon) source.

cpa.reason: Not primarily a compensation pattern (joint OA) — Foot Intrinsics (abductor hallucis) facilitation supports remaining function but doesn't reverse the joint change. Fascial component (from source): Plantar plate / 1st-ray fascia.

kineticChain.name: First MTP Extension — Hallux Mobility
kineticChain.chainEffect: The direct match: "severely restricted, <20° / hallux rigidus ... patient walks on lateral foot border" is this app's own description of this exact condition.

functionalScreen.reason: No dedicated forefoot/hallux FMA test exists in this app's library — the grind test and passive ROM (above) remain the primary tools. FMA source note: 1st-MTP dorsiflexion loss on toe-off; grind test.

Swelling/tenderness of 1st MTP.text: Acute swelling and tenderness over the first MTP joint reflects capsuloligamentous injury to the plantar plate and collateral ligament complex from a forced hyperextension mechanism — an acute injury pattern distinct from the chronic bony change of hallux rigidus.

athlete.text: This injury classically occurs in athletes on artificial turf or other firm playing surfaces, where a fixed forefoot combined with an axial load through a raised heel drives the MTP joint into forced hyperextension — the mechanism that gives turf toe its name.

Push-off avoidance posture.text: Avoiding terminal MTP extension during push-off protects the injured plantar plate/capsule from the exact end-range loading that reproduces pain, functionally similar to the push-off avoidance seen in hallux rigidus but arising from an acute sprain rather than a chronic degenerative block.

Plantar plate / sesamoid.text: Tenderness over the plantar plate and sesamoid complex localizes the injury to the primary structures stressed during forced hyperextension, and should prompt imaging to exclude a concurrent sesamoid fracture.

findings: Resisted great-toe flexion may be weak/painful if the plantar plate/FHL is involved
Passive 1st MTP dorsiflexion STRESS reproduces pain — an acute sprain pattern, not the chronic restriction seen in hallux rigidus
sttt.interpretation: Passive 1st MTP dorsiflexion stress reproducing pain reflects an acute capsuloligamentous sprain (turf toe), distinct from the chronic restriction seen in hallux rigidus; weak/painful resisted great-toe flexion suggests plantar plate/FHL involvement.

cpa.pattern: FHL may show acute reflex inhibition post-injury — reassess once the sprain has settled. Fascial component (from source): Plantar plate / sesamoid complex.

kineticChain.name: First MTP Extension — Hallux Mobility (use cautiously)
kineticChain.chainEffect: This test targets the OPPOSITE direction from this injury's mechanism (chronic restriction vs. an acute hyperextension sprain) — use cautiously and only once acute pain allows.

functionalScreen.reason: No dedicated forefoot/hallux FMA test exists in this app's library — the dorsiflexion stress test (above) remains the primary tool. FMA source note: 1st-MTP dorsiflexion stress reproduces pain; toe-off deficit.

Dorsal midfoot swelling/tenderness.text: Swelling and tenderness over the dorsal navicular, cuboid, or tarsometatarsal joints reflects capsuloligamentous injury or degenerative change at the midfoot articulations; its dorsal, joint-line location helps distinguish a routine midfoot sprain from a Lisfranc fracture-dislocation, which requires urgent weight-bearing imaging when the mechanism or severity warrants.

Collapsed or rigid midfoot posture.text: A collapsed midfoot reflects ligamentous laxity or instability of the midtarsal joints, while a rigid midfoot reflects degenerative stiffening — both patterns lie along the spectrum from midfoot sprain to osteoarthritis and help direct which structures are prioritized on exam.

Navicular.text: Point tenderness over the navicular localizes to the talonavicular joint or the navicular tuberosity (the tibialis posterior insertion), a common site of both traumatic and degenerative midfoot pathology.

Cuboid.text: Tenderness over the cuboid may reflect cuboid subluxation ("cuboid syndrome") or calcaneocuboid joint pathology, a distinct but related midfoot pain generator from navicular-based pathology.

TMT joints.text: Tenderness at the tarsometatarsal (Lisfranc) joints localizes injury or degeneration to the midfoot-forefoot junction; marked tenderness here following a high-energy mechanism should prompt weight-bearing imaging to exclude a Lisfranc fracture-dislocation.

findings: Resisted inversion/eversion is less specific for midfoot pathology
Passive midfoot stress / piano-key glide (joint-play) is the definitive provocation
sttt.interpretation: Resisted inversion/eversion is less specific here; the passive midfoot stress / piano-key glide (joint-play) test is the definitive provocation for navicular/cuboid midfoot pathology.

muscles.name: Tibialis Posterior
muscles.state: Secondary guarding — screen once acute pain allows

muscles.name: Peroneals
muscles.state: Secondary guarding — screen once acute pain allows

cpa.pattern: Tibialis Posterior and Peroneals can secondarily guard around a stiff or unstable midfoot — screen both once acute pain allows. Fascial component (from source): Midfoot dorsal & plantar fascia.

kineticChain.reason: Not covered by this app's foot/ankle kinetic-chain tests (talocrural, subtalar, and hallux are modelled; the midtarsal joints are not) — rely on the passive midfoot-stress test above.

functionalScreen.name: Single Leg Balance (adjunct — no dedicated midfoot screen exists)
functionalScreen.note: No dedicated midfoot FMA test exists in this app's library — Single Leg Balance can surface secondary instability once acute pain allows. FMA source note: Midfoot stress / piano-key & single-leg load reproduce pain.
